page: Google Cloud Platform n1-standard-8 is a general-purpose virtual machine belonging to the N1 server family. It features 8 dedicated vCPUs mapped to 4 physical Intel Xeon cores running at 2.3 GHz, with hyper-threading enabled. The instance is configured with 30 GB of x86_64 system memory, yielding 3.75 GB of RAM per core. It does not include local NVMe storage or bundled GPUs, and provides zero complimentary public IPv4 addresses.

Benchmark results indicate that the n1-standard-8 delivers modest processing capabilities. Single-core and multi-core CPU performance in stress-ng tests falls into the bottom 25%, while Geekbench single-core scores are in the bottom 10%. Memory bandwidth for large uncached blocks is average, though small-block cached read bandwidth is weak. Cryptographic and compression workloads, such as gzip and bzip3, register in the bottom 10% to 25% tiers. However, the instance achieves average performance in Geekbench ray tracing and LLM text generation for small 135M models.

From a qualitative cost-efficiency perspective, the n1-standard-8 represents an older hardware generation with lower resource density compared to newer architectures. It is suitable for workloads that require dedicated vCPUs but do not demand high-performance computing, such as basic web serving, light database operations, and general-purpose utility tasks.
description: Google Cloud Platform n1-standard-8 is an x86_64 general-purpose server from the N1 family, equipped with 8 dedicated Intel Xeon vCPUs (4 physical cores with hyper-threading) running at 2.3 GHz and 30 GB of RAM. It contains no local storage or GPUs. Performance benchmarks position this instance primarily in the lower tiers, with single-core and multi-core CPU performance, database operations, and static web serving throughput falling into the bottom 25%. However, it maintains average performance in large-block memory bandwidth and small-model LLM text generation. Given its older hardware profile, the n1-standard-8 is best suited for moderate, non-intensive workloads such as basic web serving, development environments, and general-purpose utility tasks where dedicated CPU allocation is required but peak performance is not critical.
